progression.prerequisiteKnowledge: From bio-m5-b06a: bacteria carry plasmids. From bio-m5-b06b: RNA polymerase binds a promoter before a gene and copies the gene into mRNA. From bio-m5-b06c: ribosomes read mRNA three bases at a time (codons), each coding for an amino acid. From bio-m5-b04: DNA's two strands are held together by base pairs (A with T, C with G) along a sugar-phosphate backbone. From Year 11: enzymes are specific. From b09: recombinant DNA means DNA joined from different sources; bacteria make human insulin (since 1982); Bt cotton carries a gene from a soil bacterium. From b16: gene cloning puts a gene into a plasmid vector, a bacterial host copies it every time it divides; a colony is a clone. From bio-m6-b05: many genes contain introns, stretches cut out of the mRNA before translation. Not assumed: restriction enzymes, sticky ends, ligase, marker genes, transformation, selection, why a host needs a promoter it recognises, Agrobacterium, "transgenic" by name.
progression.startsWith: A DNA fragment and a vector. The video opens: Bacteria don't make human insulin, and cotton plants don't make a caterpillar poison.
progression.stopsAfter: explaining why an intron-free copy of a human gene is needed for bacteria (bacteria cannot remove introns), made from mRNA or built from scratch, as for the first insulin; describing in order how recombinant DNA is made and put into a host: a restriction enzyme cuts at one specific sequence, leaving sticky ends, and the plasmid is opened with the same enzyme or one that leaves matching ends; the ends pair and DNA ligase seals the backbones, making recombinant DNA; the plasmid carries a marker gene; bacteria take up the plasmid by transformation (calcium chloride helps DNA stick to the cell surface, then a heat shock lets it in), only a small fraction of them; antibiotic selection keeps bacteria with a plasmid, and a second check finds those carrying the gene; explaining that the host makes the protein only if the gene sits beside a promoter the host recognises, and that the shared genetic code means the same codons give the same amino acids; describing the insulin application (two chains made separately in bacteria, joined, made in large fermenters) and the agricultural application (plants need a different carrier because of the cell wall and because the gene must enter the plant's chromosomes; Agrobacterium carries the Bt gene into cotton cells' chromosomes, and the cells grow into whole plants that pass it on in their seeds); defining a transgenic organism (the contrast with selective breeding is in key note 5 only); applying this to an unseen describe item and an unseen explain item.
progression.nextLesson: which benefits of genetic technologies in agriculture, medicine and industry hold up under evidence (route entry bio-m6-b19).

teaching.task: Bacteria don't make human insulin, and cotton doesn't make a caterpillar poison, yet both now do. So how do scientists cut out a useful piece of DNA, join it into a carrier, get it into a host, and make sure the host actually uses it?
teaching.causalExplanation: Causes: why an intron-free copy is needed (bacteria cannot remove introns, 2); why sticky ends join (unpaired bases pair with matching bases, 3); why ligase is needed (pairing alone gives only weak bonds; the backbone stays open, 4); why the marker matters (only bacteria with a plasmid survive the antibiotic, 6); why survival is not proof (empty plasmids also carry the marker, 6); why the host makes a human protein (a promoter it recognises and a shared code, 7); why the plant needs a different carrier (the cell wall, and the gene must enter the plant's chromosomes) and how the trait reaches the seeds (Agrobacterium inserts DNA into the chromosomes; every cell carries the gene, 8). The selective breeding contrast is key note 5 only (Revision 2). Visible case: the splicing strip, the staggered cut, the clasp sealing the gaps, the two plates growing side by side, the codon read by two ribosomes. Thinking opportunities: two unseen items. Reading load: at most about three bright text items; attempt 2's card is the densest frame and is the task.
teaching.conversationalApproach: Bacteria now make human insulin and cotton makes a caterpillar poison, so the question is how scientists cut out a useful piece of DNA, join it into a carrier, get it into a host and make sure the host uses it. A station track follows the method one step at a time: get intron-free DNA because bacteria cannot remove introns, cut with a restriction enzyme that recognises one short sequence and leaves sticky ends, paste with sticky-end pairing sealed by DNA ligase, put the plasmid into bacteria with calcium chloride and a heat shock, and pick the hosts on antibiotic agar; using the gene needs a promoter the host recognises, and plants need Agrobacterium to carry the gene across the cell wall into the plant's chromosomes. The memory aid is cut, paste, put in, pick. Two exam questions follow with brief feedback.
teaching.openingDecision: Bacteria don't make human insulin, and cotton plants don't make a caterpillar poison. Yet since the nineteen-eighties, bacteria have made human insulin for people with diabetes, and most Australian cotton now makes its own insect toxin. Both carry DNA from another species. So how do scientists cut out a useful piece of DNA, join it into a carrier, get it into a host, and make sure the host actually uses it?
teaching.understandingCheck: 10a is a describe item: scientists have an intron-free copy of the calf gene for chymosin and a plasmid with an ampicillin-resistance gene; describe how they could produce E. coli carrying the chymosin gene and identify those bacteria. It tests the whole chain in order on a new product. 10c is an explain item: a human gene copied directly from a chromosome gives a faulty protein in bacteria, while a copy made from the same gene's mRNA gives a working one; explain the results. It tests scene 2's and scene 7's causes. Each ends "Pause here to answer." with a 10 s countdown; the full card stays on screen during and after the countdown. Each feedback is brief (about 25 to 30 s): the answer, the key reason, the givens underlined in the question strip as they are used, one crossed-out classic mistake. No givens card.
teaching.curriculumScope: B6-IQ3-04: "describe techniques and applications used in recombinant DNA technology, for example:" with its example "the development of transgenic organisms in agricultural and medical applications (ACSBL087)". This video owns full coverage of B6-IQ3-04: techniques (obtaining intron-free DNA, restriction enzymes, ligase, vectors, transformation, selection, expression) and applications (insulin-making bacteria in medicine; Bt cotton in agriculture; chymosin in attempt 1). It also completes B6-IQ3-01 for recombinant DNA (use and advantage: a trait or product from another species in one generation). Update the ledger rows when this design passes review. The verbs: "describe" (what-markers-reward: give characteristics and features, in order, with the tool responsible at each step) is carried by scenes 3 to 6 and attempt 1; "explain" (cause and effect) by scenes 2 and 7 and attempt 2.

design.visualSystem: One toolchain bench: a horizontal track of five stations across the top of the screen, filled left to right one per scene, each with a small painted object or coded tool and a one-word grey label: "get the DNA" (scene 2), "cut" (scene 3), "paste" (scene 4), "put in" (scene 5), "pick" (scene 6), then "use" (scene 7) as a sixth station that slides in. The active station enlarges into the main stage below; finished stations shrink to grey thumbnails on the track. DNA is coded throughout in b01's `SlimStrand` style: a double strand of cream base glyphs on two backbone lines, with the useful gene as an amber stretch and the plasmid as a teal ring, never base letters spoken. Enzymes are small coded shapes in the explainer style (restriction enzyme: a slate scissor-jaw blob; ligase: an ochre clasp blob), labelled once. Painted plates for real things: `m6-bacteriophage-t4-v1.png` (scene 3), `m6-bacterium-plasmid-v1.png`, `m6-plasmid-uptake-start-v1.png` and `-end-v1.png` (scene 5), new `m6-water-bath-tube-v1.png` (scene 5), new `m6-antibiotic-colonies-empty-v1.png` with the existing `m6-antibiotic-colonies-before-v1.png` and `-after-v1.png` (scene 6; an aligned set: the empty dish grows into the crowded dish on the "no antibiotic" plate and into the sparse dish on the "with antibiotic" plate, side by side; never a crowded-to-sparse crossfade), `m6-agar-dish-top-v1.png`, `m6-insulin-vial-v1.png`, new `m6-fermenter-tank-v1.png` (scene 7), `m6-bt-cotton-v1.png`, `b6a-plant-cell-v1.png` and `m6-tissue-culture-jars-v1.png` (scene 8), `b6a-bacterium-v1.png` (Agrobacterium glyph source, tinted). No people, no hands. Never used: `m6-hand-pollination-v1.png` and `m6-agricultural-liming-v1.png` (retired hand plates). Plates scale proportionally, never stretched. Clutter rule (owner, 19 Oct): at most about three bright text items at once besides the small grey station labels; each tag fades when the next cue lands; completed stations dim to grey.
